analysis.headline: Passed the House 224-194 on February 6, 2020, but was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on February 10, 2020, and never received a Senate vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The PRO Act would overhaul federal labor law to make it easier for workers to join unions and bargain collectively. It would expand who counts as an 'employee' under the law, ban forced anti-union meetings, impose new penalties on employers who fire or retaliate against workers for organizing, invalidate agreements that force workers out of class actions, speed up union elections, and allow union 'fair share' fee agreements to override state right-to-work laws. The House passed it, but the Senate never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who want to organize or join a union, workers currently covered by union contracts, and employees misclassified as independent contractors. Roughly all private-sector workers gain stronger protections against being fired or penalized for organizing, and workers who organize would gain double-damages remedies and access to class litigation.

how_it_helps.text: Broadens the definitions of 'employee,' 'supervisor,' and 'employer' to prevent employers from classifying workers as exempt from labor law protections, using an ABC test for independent contractor status.

Makes it an unfair labor practice to require or coerce employees to attend employer meetings designed to discourage union membership, and to permanently replace or discriminate against workers who participate in strikes.
Prohibits employers from entering into agreements under which employees waive the right to pursue or join collective or class-action litigation.

Expands remedies for workers harmed by labor violations to include back pay without reduction, consequential damages, liquidated damages equal to two times actual damages, punitive damages, and civil penalties of up to $50,000 per violation (up to $100,000 for repeat violations), plus a new private right of action allowing workers to sue employers directly.

Revises union election procedures: employers would be barred from participating in NLRB representation proceedings, must provide voter lists to petitioning unions, and must begin bargaining if a union wins a majority of votes; election timelines are compressed to days rather than weeks.

Allows collective-bargaining agreements to require all employees in a bargaining unit to contribute fees to the union for representation costs, notwithstanding state law to the contrary, and removes whistleblower protections and injunction limits so courts can more quickly restrain employer violations causing discharge or serious economic harm.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, particularly those in industries that actively contest union organizing. The bill creates civil penalties up to $50,000-$100,000 per unfair labor practice violation, double damages plus punitive damages, director and officer liability, a private right of action with attorney's fees, and bans on mandatory anti-union meetings and forced arbitration of labor claims [S4][S5]. Employers would also lose their standing to participate in NLRB representation proceedings and lose the right to sue unions over secondary strikes [S4][S5]. Companies relying on independent contractor models (for example, gig platforms) would face reclassification pressure under the new employee definition [S4][S5].

drawbacks.text: The bill overrides state right-to-work laws: fair-share fee agreements would be enforceable notwithstanding any state law, meaning workers in right-to-work states could be required to pay union fees as a condition of employment even if their state forbids it.

It permits secondary strikes — union members pressuring workers of a different employer during a dispute — and terminates employers' right to bring claims against unions that conduct such secondary strikes, which opponents argue exposes neutral third-party businesses to labor disputes they are not party to.

The ABC test for independent contractor status and broadened joint-employer definition could disrupt business models built on independent contractors and franchise structures, including gig work arrangements, by sweeping those workers into mandatory bargaining structures.
Employers would have no standing as a party in NLRB representation proceedings, removing their ability to contest proposed bargaining units or election procedures before a vote occurs.

For a first union contract, unresolved disputes after 120 days would go to binding arbitration by a tripartite panel, whose decision would bind the parties for two years — opponents argue this removes the employer's ability to negotiate or say no to terms it cannot afford.

New penalties and litigation exposure raise compliance costs for all covered employers, including small businesses, since the bill sets no small-business exemption in its penalty and civil-action provisions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would meaningfully strengthen workers' ability to organize and bargain, with remedies and penalties that give labor law real teeth for the first time in decades; workers who are fired for organizing would for the first time recover double damages and be able to sue directly. The costs fall on employers, especially those whose business practices depend on resisting organizing, misclassifying workers, or using forced arbitration. The genuinely contested trade-offs are the preemption of state right-to-work laws — which forces fees on objecting workers in those states — and the removal of employer participation in union elections and first-contract binding arbitration, which shift decision-making power heavily toward unions. The design is ambitious and one-sided toward labor, but the core protections against retaliation and misclassification address widely documented gaps in current law.

outcome.mechanism: Passed the House on a recorded vote of 224-194 (Roll no. 50) on February 6, 2020; received in the Senate and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on February 10, 2020, where no further action was taken before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: Introduced May 2, 2019 by Rep. Bobby Scott (D-VA) with 218 cosponsors (216 Democrats, 2 Republicans).
The House Committee on Education and Labor ordered the bill reported on a 26-21 vote on September 25, 2019, and reported it amended on December 16, 2019 (H. Rept. 116-347).
The House passed the bill 224-194 on February 6, 2020 (Roll no. 50), with 219 Democrats, 5 Republicans, and 0 independents in favor, and 186 Republicans, 7 Democrats, and 1 independent opposed.
A motion to recommit with instructions to bar labor organizations from communicating with unauthorized workers failed 195-223 (Roll no. 49).

The bill was received in the Senate on February 10, 2020, read twice, and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions; the Senate took no further action during the remainder of the 116th Congress.
